newsitem.title: GERMANY: Market jitters send German shares lower at close.
newsitem.headline: Market jitters send German shares lower at close.

text.p: The Frankfurt bourse closed lower on Wednesday with worries creeping back into the market of a fresh fall on Wall Street later in the day.
Dealers said the fact that the U.S. S&P futures index was down, suggesting Wall Street will open lower, was worrying the market, along with losses on Asian markets overnight.
"The S&P contract has been doing funny things overnight and that has spooked some people," said one trader.
The DAX index of 30 top German shares, ended down 49.95 points, or 1.73 percent, at 2,841.05.
The DAX had closed on Tuesday at 2,891 points, almost recouping all the losses posted on Friday following a bout of global market jitters.
Dealers said the fall on Friday, promted by comments by Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan about "irrational exuberance" in global asset markets, was still causing nerves.
"Greenspan is still making people edgy. We are extra-sensitive to any move down," said one trader.
Dealers said that a Wall Street Journal article suggesting that a slowdown in Japanese purchases of U.S. debt could depress U.S. markets had also prompted fears.
Losses were spread across the board, with export-oriented chemicals and auto stocks especially hard hit as the dollar moved towards 1.54 marks, down a pfennig on Tuesday's level.
Shares in chemical company BASF AG ended bourse trade down 1.68 marks, almost three percent, at 60.50 marks, while chemical group Bayer AG fell 2.46 marks, almost four percent to 62.09 marks.

Meanwhile, shares in chemicals and drugs company Hoechst AG ended down five pfennigs at 70.85, less than the market trend and much less than other chemical stocks after the firm made a buy out bid for French pharmaceuticals group Roussel Uclaf.
The stock had risen to a record high on Tuesday after the firm said it had merged its speciality chemicals division with the Swiss group Clariant AG.
Dealers said the market focus would turn to key inflation data due out of the U.S. later in the day, particularly in the light of worries following Greenspan's comments.
The market is particularly eager to see the U.S. November producer prices, forecast to show a 0.3 percent rise after climbing 0.4 percent in October.
